In testimony on Thursday, Mr. Williams, who has been given a guarantee that his cooperation will exempt him from prosecution, described loans and gifts, including a $20,000 shopping spree in New York City for Ms. McDonnell. Defense lawyers have just begun to subject his account to cross-examination.
Ms. McDonnell’s defense team argued in opening statements that she accepted Mr. Williams’s gifts because she had a “crush” on Mr. Williams and was hungry for his attention. She promoted Anatabloc aggressively, her lawyers said, because of a longstanding interest in nutritional supplements. The two exchanged more than 1,200 emails and texts.
Asked by the prosecution whether he and Ms. McDonnell had been romantically involved, Mr. Williams said no. “It was a business relationship,” he said.
He described attending a charity dinner at Ms. McDonnell’s request, at which one of the items being auctioned to raise money was a trip to New York with the governor and his wife. Mr. Williams said he was the only bidder. “I bid against myself,” he said, until the price reached about $12,000.
When the trial resumes on Friday, Mr. Williams will face cross-examination from lawyers for both McDonnells.
Late on Thursday, he described how he first realized that his relationship with the couple was under investigation by the F.B.I. and state police. In early 2013, a large box arrived at his home near Richmond. It contained the Oscar de la Renta dresses he had bought Ms. McDonnell to wear to her husband’s inauguration and to the couple’s 35th wedding anniversary celebrations. Mr. Williams had “a sinking feeling,” he said. “It was like, ‘Oh no.’ ”
Enclosed was a handwritten letter from Ms. McDonnell, explaining that she was returning the dresses as they had always agreed so that the Williamses’ daughter could have them or they could be auctioned for charity.
“I sat down in a chair in the den and read the letter over and over,” Mr. Williams said. “This letter was a fabrication.”
He immediately called his lawyer.
Correction: July 31, 2014
Because of an editing error, an earlier version of this article misstated the day Jonnie R. Williams Sr. testified about loans and gifts including a $20,000 shopping spree. It was Thursday, not Monday.

Hillary Rodham Clinton’s coming memoir about her tenure as Secretary of State will be titled “Hard Choices,” her publisher said early Friday.
The title speaks to the dilemma Mrs. Clinton faced at the State Department, carrying out President Obama’s vision of diplomacy while bringing her own more hawkish stance to foreign policy discussions.
Lately, as Mrs. Clinton emerges as a potential 2016 presidential candidate, she has been pushed to more clearly define her legacy as secretary of state. When she was asked recently at an event in New York what her proudest accomplishment was at the State Department her response lacked specifics and set off criticism.
“I think we really restored America’s leadership in the best sense,” Mrs. Clinton said. Then, she added that people could read all about the specifics of her record in
her book
.
Mrs. Clinton’s push for an apology to the Pakistanis, her work getting the Iranians to the negotiating table, her brokering of a cease-fire in Gaza and her efforts to open up Burma are expected to be central to the book’s narrative. Ted Widmer, a former White House speechwriter, was one of the aides who assisted Mrs. Clinton in her research and writing.
“Hard Choices,” which Simon & Schuster is publishing, will be released on June 10. For her previous book “Living History,” about her time as first lady, Mrs. Clinton received a near-record $9 million advance and broke nonfiction sales records.
The advance on her new book is said to be less.

Episode 5:
‘King of Norway’
(Though Really, the Title Should Be ‘Surprise!’)
We start the latest installment of HBO’s “Boardwalk Empire” with another flashback – except this one doesn’t go quite as far back as those earlier in the season. It’s Atlantic City, 1897, and a young deputy sheriff has been sent to check out a dead body under the old iron pier. It turns out the body’s not human, but porcine. When the complainant – Mrs. Zeller, an ornery old woman – asks who this deputy is, he says the name’s Enoch Thompson. No kidding. This actor (Marc Pickering) is a dead ringer for a young Steve Buscemi. (He also has Mr. Buscemi’s mannerisms as the adult Nucky Thompson down cold.)
'Boardwalk Empire'
‘Boardwalk Empire’ Recap: Surprise, Surprise
‘Boardwalk Empire’ Recap: Paying the Price
‘Boardwalk Empire’ Recap: ‘Jesus Was Wrong’
Cut to Capone (Stephen Graham) on the can, reading the paper. He’s constipated and agitated. Capone comes out and says he spoke to Nucky about Luciano’s plot against him, but all Nucky had to say was: “History doesn’t repeat itself. But it does rhyme.” (Which Nucky
stole from Mark Twain
.)
Capone calls it “a message — like an omen.” He obviously has never read Twain. He knows he’s being investigated for income tax evasion – facing a minimum of five years in prison —  and announces that they have to move the entire operation out of Chicago, to nearby Cicero, by the next day. D’Angelo (Louis Cancelmi), the undercover agent, looks slightly alarmed. Capone picks up on it and asks him what the problem is. “You got something better to do?”
The nerdy accountant, Reese, meanwhile is upset that a big roach is crawling on his books. The bug is the least of their problems.
In 1931 A.C., the hobo kid that Mickey Doyle (Paul Sparks) picked to unload trucks one night comes into Nucky’s office all cleaned up. He’s Doyle’s assistant now, this Joe Harper, and he tells Nucky that Mickey needs to see him. (Isn’t it a little late in the show to be introducing completely new characters?) When Nucky pulls the door open, Chalky (Michael Kenneth Williams) is also sitting there, wearing a three-piece suit and that frown of his. Surprise! Chalky says he’s not packing: He had been frisked at the door.
Nucky says, “That wouldn’t stop a man who’s made up his mind.”
Nucky offers him a drink, but Chalky declines. “Doesn’t anyone drink anymore?” Nucky asks.
When he asks Chalky what he’s been up to, he says he “ran with some boys” and then mumbles something about a gas station and getting left behind. “Done some time,” he says.
“I heard you were still doing it,” Nucky shoots back.
Nucky apologizes and says he doesn’t know where Narcisse (Jeffrey Wright) is. But he does know that Chalky’s family moved to St. Louis and is living under the wife’s maiden name. He offers Chalky a place to hide out and tells him he should start over.
“We ain’t schoolboys no more,” Chalky says. (Ah, but in the flashbacks they were.)
Nucky peels off some money for him, and though Chalky at first refuses, Nucky insists: “This is between friends.”
Suddenly, we’re inside one of Eli’s nightmares again, which includes a yodeling record and a portrait of a mustached man. Drunk again. There’s a knock at the door, which awakens Eli (Shea Whigham). It’s his wife, June (Nisi Sturgis), who’s been waiting at the station for Eli to show up. She’s visiting Chicago from A.C. and is — surprise! — seven months pregnant. It’s been that long since they’ve seen each other.
Eli is shocked at, but thrilled with, her condition.
When she has the baby, Eli says, June should move to Chicago with the newborn and two youngest kids, because he needs her. “It’s a blessing, a chance to start over,” he says. “Not everyone gets that.”
After a makeout session, Eli tells June they’ve been invited to his partner’s house for a home-cooked meal. Where other surprises await.
Gillian (Gretchen Mol), meanwhile, is still passing her days at the insane asylum. Her crazy friend, Charlotte, runs in and urgently hands her a piece of paper and tells her, “Protect your fur.” Charlotte is dragged out by the matrons. The urgent piece of paper is an ad for Saks fur storage. Is this some kind of secret message – like Capone’s Twain message — or is Charlotte just crazy? I lay 10-to-1 odds on just plain crazy.
Next, Nucky is meeting with Johnny Torrio (Greg Antonacci) in Brooklyn about Luciano (Vincent Piazza) wanting to get him. Torrio says, “It don’t make sense.” Torrio seems slightly confused and preoccupied. He’s either losing his mind, too, or is up to something. I lay 10-to-1 odds on up to something. He again tells Nucky he should retire, then offers to meet with him and Maranzano (Giampiero Judica) to see what’s up.
In another flashback, Nucky is meeting with his boss, Sheriff Lindsay (Boris McGiver). The sheriff tells Nucky he likes his girl, Mabel, but Nucky says Mabel’s father (Burke Moses) doesn’t like him. To win him over, Nucky is taking him to the fancy new Oyster House. (
Dock’s Oyster House
, the real deal on Atlantic Avenue, actually opened in 1897 and is still in operation. The same family that opened Dock’s, the Doughertys, eventually bought
the legendary Knife & Fork
as well, which the real Commodore helped found.)
Nucky bumps into Pat Halligan (Danny McCarthy), the guy who lost his hat long ago, the one that Nucky retrieved and returned  at the Corner Hotel when he was a boy. Halligan has just left a meeting with the Commodore. “How’s the hat game these days?” Halligan asks. “Sailing right along, sir,” Nucky answers.
The sheriff and Nucky go into their meeting with the Commodore (John Ellison Conlee) and Leander (a younger version of the
Dominic Chianese’s character
with the crazy white facial hair.) (Remember, for the record, that Mr. Chianese, the actor, worked with Lansky in Havana in “The Godfather: Part II.” But that’s neither here nor there. Back to our story.)
Halligan, they explain, is trying to renegotiate a longstanding agreement with the Commodore, putting on the “squeeze from New York.” The Commodore is angry and says he doesn’t want to see Halligan or his cronies around.
Nucky suggests deputizing about 20 men and placing them at the train stations, ferries and hotels. “Anyone we don’t like the look of,” he says, “see them off.” (This was actually done by Mayor Frank Hague in Jersey City, where his zeps – or secret police – would patrol the streets and escort anyone they didn’t like out of the city.) There’s nothing illegal about it, Leander says, “Just enforcing the vagrancy laws.”
At dinner at Van Alden’s house, Eli and June are trying to be polite, but the Van Alden clan seems unusually cranky, even for them. When young Chester tries to entertain the guests with his recorder, Van Alden (Michael Shannon) snaps, “Chester, that would sound better much further away.” Eli is telling Van Alden not to worry about Luciano’s having recognized him. “He can’t prove anything,” Eli says.
But Val Alden is worried and says that they’ll go after Eli, too, since he’s his partner. “You’ll fold,” he tells Eli.
When June compliments Van Alden on the house, his Norwegian wife, Sigrid (Christiane Seidel), complains about the leaky roof. June offers to have Eli come over and help Van Alden fix it. Sigrid seems especially agitated, and she insults her husband even more than usual, saying that one man – Eli – is enough for the job. She says that he should come over when her husband is not home (wink wink).
Back in New York City, it seems that Margaret (
Kelly Macdonald
) has persuaded Carolyn Rothstein (Jennifer Ferrin) to take the deal she and Nucky have offered. At a meeting with the firm’s partners and her lawyer, Carolyn signs off and Margaret hands over the check – written out from Old Rumpus Associates. Carolyn’s lawyer puts up a fuss because of the company’s ridiculous name and its location out of state. “This is the deal,” Margaret says. “The only deal.” Carolyn snatches the check, folds it and sticks it in her wallet.
Afterward, Margaret’s big boss begins to chastise her for having been secretly married all this time and associating with criminals. But he’s really eager to thank Nucky personally. Margaret, cool as an oyster on ice at Dock’s, directs her boss to set up an account for Nucky under an assumed name, to be used for shorting the stock of the Mayflower Grain Corporation. Who’s bossing whom now? She’ll be running that firm in no time.
Back in Atlantic City, a United States marshal shows up at the Old Rumpus looking for Albert White, a.k.a. Chalky. He’s on the run, the marshal says, after killing a prison guard and the convict he escaped with. He asks Mickey if he’s seen him, a “colored fella” with a big scar on his face. There might even be a reward. Mickey leads him into the kitchen, where a black man in a suit is turned with his back to them. “Albert White,” the marshal says, drawing his gun, “Put down the knife and raise your hands.” When the man turns around, it’s not Chalky, but another African-American man with a big scar on his face. “Name’s Jenkins, sir.”
“It’s not him,” the marshal says. The marshal turns and leaves, then Chalky steps out from the kitchen.
“Oh,” Mickey laughs. “There you are.”
Eli and June are helping clean up after dinner at Van Alden’s, and suddenly, Eli sees the picture of the man who was in his dream earlier. It’s a portrait of the king of Norway, hanging in the kitchen. Eli has his own flashback, (complete with a yodeling soundtrack), of having sex with Sigrid in this very kitchen.
“You remember now,” Sigrid says. She calls everyone in the room a liar and announces that she and Eli have had sex (though she uses the premium cable verb, much to her young daughter’s horror and Van Alden’s surprise). June punches Eli in the stomach.
But that’s not the only after-dinner surprise, folks. D’Angelo shows up and flashes his badge. “Let’s take a ride,” he tells Van Alden. “You too, Sheriff Thompson.” Worst. Dinner. Party. Ever.
Back at the insane asylum, one woman is cradling a shoe like a baby. Another is shivering on the floor. Still another shouts about butter and runs through the room. Gillian sits calmly, smoking a cigarette. She’s the odd girl out. Her friend, Charlotte, is wheeled in, looking subdued. Too subdued. Has she been given a lobotomy?
“Dr. Cotton?” Gillian asks her. “What did he do to you?” She won’t answer. “Is it your mouth? Did he …” Gillian asks.
But Charlotte opens her gown and reveals a giant, bloody incision across her abdomen. “The sickness,” she says, “was someplace else.”
Young Nucky is having dinner at the Oyster House with his future father-in-law, explaining how he plans to make good right here in A.C. No need to go to Alaska for the gold rush. The city, Nucky explains, has doubled in size over a decade. There are 10,000 tourists every day in the summer. And he’s working his way up the ladder of success.
“From bellboy to deputy sheriff,” the father says.
“Every story has a beginning, sir,” Nucky says. And this is it.
The father sends Mabel for some smokes and tells Nucky what he really thinks of him. “I don’t know what she sees in you,” he says. “I think you talk a bold line … but I don’t think you know what you are.”
“Well I suppose, sir,” Nucky answers, “that we’ll both find that out.”
Cut to the Cuban bodyguard (Paul Calderón), warily standing watch at the New York restaurant where Nucky is meeting with Maranzano. They’ve been waiting for Torrio but decide to go ahead with business. Nucky asks when he will get rid of Luciano.
“He disappoints me, that is true,” Maranzano says.
“He’ll come for me again,” Nucky says, “and then he’ll come for you.”
“When one sits on the throne, that is to be expected,” Maranzano explains.
A car pulls up with two machine-gun toting gangsters, who open fire, shattering the windows. The bodyguard covers Nucky and pushes him to the floor to safety, but it seems most everyone else is Swiss cheese. It’s not clear if Maranzano is dead or not. (In real life, Luciano had Maranzano shot and stabbed in 1931 inside Maranzano’s office in what is now the Helmsley Building on Park Avenue.  Morbid gangster fans like me can find actual photos of Maranzano’s dead body online.)
In another flashback, Nucky knocks on the sheriff’s door late at night. “The jobs you do for the Commodore — that have their own rules — I can help with those,” he offers. The sheriff tells him to go home and that they’ll talk about it another time.
Gillian, in an obvious panic from seeing Charlotte’s nasty incision, is meeting with Dr. Cotton, the butcher, to calmly tell him personally that she has made a full recovery and is ready to talk about her release.
“I took someone’s life in a state of temporary insanity out of grief,” she explains.
“You know you were ill —  and now you know you’re not?” the doctor asks. “How? How do you know what you are?”
“How do you know?” she shoots back. Crazy as a fox, that Gillian.
“Where does insanity go?” he muses. Other illnesses re-emerge and are in the body forever unless they’re routed out.
“We’ll find what’s inside you,” he promises. “We’ll fix it.”
Gillian needs a Plan B. Pronto.
In an interrogation room, Eli is asking Van Alden not to stare at him. “The event you’re thinking about?” Eli says. “It was an accident.”
“You mean like a streetcar hitting a horse? A man getting his head crushed in a metal press? A gas explosion in which bystanders are literally torn limb from limb? That’s what your having sexual relations with my wife was like?” Van Alden gets all the best lines these days.
“I don’t know about you,” Eli says, “but my life is a” — insert another cable-ready adjective  — “shipwreck.”
“Well, land ho,” Van Alden says. Ha!
D’Angelo and an associate walk in and run down their capital crimes, then tell them how they’re going to cooperate or get the gas chamber. D’Angelo gives them the key to Capone’s count room and the combination to the safe. They tell Eli and Van Alden to bring them the ledger books. Tonight is a good night, since there will be some Hollywood folks visiting Capone.
When Van Alden tells them those ledgers are written in code, D’Angelo shows him the solution. The accountant, Reese, he says, has agreed to cooperate.
“He’s screwy about bugs,” Eli says.
D’Angelo opens the closet door, where the accountant is bound and gagged, bugs crawling all over him. I hate gratuitous bug violence.
Torrio, Luciano and Lansky (Anatol Yusef) are meeting at Torrio’s house, telling him about the slaughter. “No telling who’s dead and who’s alive,” Lansky says.
Torrio asks who the shooters were. “Better you don’t know — keep out of it,” Luciano says. The phone rings. It’s Nucky, naturally.
“We waited for you, John,” says Nucky, cuts all over his head from the window shattering.
“I called,” Torrio says. “Didn’t you get the message?”
“Now I have a message for you,” Nucky says. “I will not rest until I see you in your graves.”
Flashback to the old woman again complaining about another dead body under the pier. Except this time, Nucky finds a person. Halligan. And there’s a flashback within a flashback (a film noir staple!) of Halligan offering him the hat reward money when Nucky was a kid.
Nucky is talking on the phone now to the Bacardi guy, Maxime Ronis (Lee Godart), in Cuba, who explains what happened to Sally (Patricia Arquette). “There was a dispute with the soldiers. She fired a gun. She died on the spot.”
Nucky wants names and says he’ll pay whatever it costs. (
Cuánto!
) But Ronis says there are no names.
In Harlem, Chalky shows up at Narcisse’s whorehouse. You knew he would. He pretends to be a john and is patted down because of the “ruckus a few nights back.” The doorman lets Chalky in. As he walks into the house alone, Chalky pulls a gun out of his pants. (I guess the guy didn’t do a very thorough pat down. And Chalky is a man who’s made up his mind.) He slowly turns a doorknob. Inside is a little girl, about 7 years old, just waking up on a couch.
The little girl’s mother steps into the room. It’s
Daughter Maitland
– surprise! — her face fully healed and as beautiful as ever. And this has
got
to be their daughter, with a small “d.”
Questions and talking points for the mob obsessed like me:
Will Gillian come up with a new escape plan, à la Chalky? Will she get her hands on some guns and shoot her way out of the nut house? Stranger things have happened in this show.
Will Nucky travel to Havana and kick Ronis’s teeth in? Or will he just forget about poor Sally and renew his vows with Margaret?
Will Margaret take over the company, or are there too few episodes left for that?
Is Narcisse hiding behind the couch? Will Chalky put a bullet through his devil-like beard?
Is Maranzano dead, or do we have to sit out another 1931 massacre – this time in the Helmsley Building?
Will June forgive Eli or raise their ninth child on her own? Will it be a boy or a girl? And will they start a baseball team now?
Will Capone realize Nucky stole that quotation from Twain and get even with a plagiarized Shakespearean sonnet?
Helene Stapinski
is the author of “Five-Finger Discount: A Crooked Family History,” a chronicle of New Jersey crime and corruption.

STARKVILLE, Miss. — Football can prove too provocative a subject for mixed company in Mississippi, so people here often turn to something everybody can agree on, like religion.
Thus it was when Mac Smith, a Mississippi State man, called his
Ole Miss
-loving brother-in-law last weekend after both teams had wrapped up the
most triumphant Saturday of football
this state had ever known.
“He has two small boys,” said Smith, who was ringing up orders at the Little Dooey, a barbecue spot now adorned with banners inviting ESPN, CBS and whatever other national broadcasters may have made it to the prairies of eastern Mississippi. “I said, ‘You better kiss them boys tonight because I think Jesus is coming tomorrow.' ”
Indeed, these are days of signs and wonders in Mississippi.
The Mississippi State Bulldogs, a perennially middling team and a routinely guaranteed pelt for the traditional football powers, were ranked in the top five of the Associated Press college football poll for the first time. The Bulldogs, led by a quarterback in Heisman Trophy contention, Dak Prescott, have already defeated two top-10 teams, including Texas A&M; on Oct. 4. On Saturday, the Bulldogs will face the second-ranked team in the country, the Auburn Tigers, in what will easily be the biggest football game the city of Starkville has witnessed. The crew of ESPN’s “College GameDay,” whose arrival on a campus is the formal blessing of a football program, showed up here for the first time.
But amazingly, a week earlier, the “GameDay” crew had been in another place for the first time, about 100 miles up the road in Oxford, Miss.
The University of Mississippi’s Rebels, who have so often served as a mild diversion to a truly eminent tailgating party, were having their own miraculous year. On Oct. 4, Mississippi beat old implacable Alabama, something the team had done about once in every six meetings. The celebrity guest picker whom ESPN had invited, the pop singer Katy Perry, rushed the field after the game with thousands of delirious adults, children and Ole Miss students, who tore down the goal posts and took them on a comprehensive tour of the town.
Continue reading the main story
After the victory, Ole Miss shot up in the rankings to No. 3 — tied with Mississippi State.
“It’s never been like this,” said Smith, whose daughter is making a 20-hour round trip from Oklahoma for Saturday’s game. “I’ll be honest with you, there are a lot of people around here that don’t know how to act.”
Mostly, people were in shock. Middle-aged men at the Little Dooey, which was preparing to smoke a whole hog for the “GameDay” hosts, sat around Thursday night trying to remember when they had played a game even close to this big or when ticket prices had shot this high. “Never” was the answer. The two teams had certainly never shared the cover of Sports Illustrated, as they did this week.
“Do you know at the Walmart over in Columbus, some guy came in and just bought up the entire batch?” Ralph Winton, who works for a beverage distributor, said of the magazines.

Bart Wood, the manager of the Little Dooey, shook his head and smiled. “Hay’s on the ground; got to get it while you can,” he said.
For now, with nearly two months before the two Mississippi teams meet in their annual
Thanksgiving
weekend rivalry game, both fan bases were wishing the other well. Two teams in contention for a spot in the college football playoff would raise the stakes of that game, known as the Egg Bowl, almost intolerably high.
“One team’s almost always bad, if not both,” said Andrew Howorth, a state circuit court judge who spent one semester at Mississippi State and the rest of his schooling at Ole Miss. “The bad team is almost always playing to be the spoiler. That’s just the deal.”
The excitement last weekend in Ole Miss was such that the local police stood down when the uprights of the goal posts were marched around Oxford like spoils of war, one of them stopping at a tailgating tent, circling the town square and ending up at the home of an Ole Miss graduate student named Buckner Corso.
A picture that Corso took
of the upright on the floor of his house was retweeted more than 1,000 times, even drawing the attention of the university’s athletic director, Ross Bjork, who asked that a piece of it be reserved for him.
On Sunday, a student rented an electric jigsaw from Home Depot, and the upright was cut into four- and six-inch pieces for distribution. One of the pieces is now being used as a pencil holder.
The Southeastern Conference levied a $50,000 fine on the university for fans rushing the field, which was on top of the $22,000 cost of replacing of the goal posts. The university started
a fund-raising campaign
asking fans to help out. By Friday morning, the campaign had raised $105,600. Mississippi plays at No. 14 Texas A&M; on Saturday.
Fans of Ole Miss, the state’s flagship institution, tend to hold a rather dismissive attitude toward Mississippi State, a land-grant university founded as the state’s agricultural and mechanical college. Many Ole Miss fans even suggested that the rivalry with Mississippi State fans, bless their hearts, was not really mutual.
State fans embrace the caricatures, their most cherished tradition being the deafening clanging of cowbells at football games. This would be somewhat akin to Yankees fans waving $100 bills.
“My family took the cow college mantra quite proudly,” said Burns Strider, a political consultant who grew up on a farm, in a Mississippi State household, and who undoubtedly confused people when he walked around midtown Manhattan last Saturday yelling, “Hail State.”
“We’ve been clothing and feeding Ole Miss Rebels for a long time,” he said. “I need doctors and lawyers from Ole Miss from time to time. I’m glad they produce them.”
For all the good feelings across the state right now, the hard fact remained that this season of miracles was not, ultimately, going to be truly shareable.
This week, a person sitting in Starkville City Hall could hear extended conversations about the merits of Ole Miss’s quarterback emanating from the mayor’s office. The mayor, Parker Wiseman, knew that his city had never been in a spotlight quite like this, and that was definitely exciting. But civic pride was not the central matter of the moment.
Sitting in his office, Wiseman read aloud a series of text messages he had sent to a friend, an Ole Miss supporter, in last Saturday’s aftermath. “I honestly never thought we’d see the likes of what we’re seeing now from either of our teams,” he had written. “Certainly I never expected it to happen simultaneously.”
“Here’s to the ride,” he continued. “May it last as long as possible. And may God protect our hearts should the Thanksgiving game actually mean something.”
